Thelonious Monk was an American jazz pianist, bandleader, and composer whose angular compositions, percussive piano technique, and uncompromising artistic vision made him one of jazz's greatest and most distinctive figures.

His highly individual style featured dissonant clusters, rhythmic displacement, and percussive attack, treating the piano as a percussion instrument rather than a melodic one. He composed innovative standards including "Round Midnight," "Straight, No Chaser," "In Walked Bud," and "Thelonious," whose angular melodies and harmonic surprises have become jazz essentials.

Monk was a bebop co-architect who developed complex harmonic language alongside Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, though his approach emphasized composerly sophistication over fleet improvisation. As a bandleader, he insisted on playing only his own compositions, refusing to participate in the jazz standard repertoire—an uncommon artistic stance that defined his independence.

He was eccentrically dressed with a distinctive personality, wearing unusual hats and engaging in mysterious silences during performances, becoming a cultural icon of jazz's avant-garde. His style was influenced by stride piano and bebop harmony, and he created a highly personal pianistic language that sounded like no one else.

John Coltrane, a saxophonist of the next generation, studied under Monk and absorbed his compositional and harmonic innovations. His compositions, marked by unexpected dissonances and structural wit, have become central to the jazz repertoire.
